query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled alloying addition of aluminum (e.g., 2–5 at.%) into the refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that serves as a diffusion barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy without significant Al content, exhibiting typical rapid oxidation at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification via the controlled addition of 2–5 at.% Al into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at approximately 1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (pure oxygen or air) for prolonged durations (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer on the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the added aluminum diffuses to the surface and oxidizes to form an Al2O3 layer. This scale is thermodynamically stable and slow-growing, which retards further oxygen ingress and overall oxidation compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (e.g., reduced weight gain per unit area and thinner oxide scales) relative to the untreated alloy under the same temperature and atmosphere conditions.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior (e.g., weight gain, oxide scale thickness) of the standard refractory high-entropy alloy without Al addition under identical exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the aluminum addition remains within a range that ensures solubility and does not compromise the high-strength or phase stability of the alloy; performance may differ in more complex transient or cycling thermal conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of an alumina scale is a well-known protective mechanism, uncertainties remain regarding the optimal Al concentration and long-term scale stability under cyclic thermal shocks which may affect performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set modified with 2–5 at.% Al and one unmodified control. Expose both sets to an oxygen-rich environment at 1200°C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, assess the samples using weight gain measurements, oxide scale thickness analysis via SEM, and phase identification via XRD.
measurements: Phase composition and morphology of the oxide layer (e.g., via XRD and SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., beyond a predetermined threshold) in oxidation behavior (weight gain and scale thickness) compared to the unmodified control, or if no continuous Al2O3 scale is detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.
